# Case Study: The Rodgers Play, and What It Changed

**What it is** — 24 December 2016, Lambeau Field, freezing, on a slow natural surface. Second and goal from the seven, 32 seconds left in the half. Myszka had worked with fifteen players on that Vikings roster; two of them are in this play.

**Everson Griffen** comes off the edge unblocked after a tactical miscue. **Aaron Rodgers** stays composed, **looking to and through** Griffen while surveying the left side, and **deliberately waits to draw Griffen closer.** When Griffen reaches what the authors call a **metastable region** — interpersonal distance around **2.5 yards** — Rodgers dips his right shoulder, turns, and arcs toward the far sideline. Mid-escape he glances over his shoulder to detect Griffen's pursuit and extends the ball away from Griffen's reaching hand.

Crossing the ten, Rodgers turns to **Xavier Rhodes**, who had been mirroring Jordy Nelson. Rodgers reads Rhodes's closing distance, speed, posture and kinematics; aims for the pylon; then **decelerates controllably over four steps, widening his base with each one** so he can cut either way. Rhodes struggles for footing, Rodgers cuts, and gets enough separation to leave nothing but a hand on him. Touchdown, Lambeau Leap, and the Vikings' season effectively ends.

**What it changed.** Myszka was already deep-diving film for weaknesses — but to make **general, global observations** about gaps, then set alive problems typical of the player's position. After this play he added a wrinkle: **use the plays where a player was stretched past their challenge point on game day to determine which problems they must spend the offseason solving.** Concretely, he now identifies **the three to five plays in a season where each player most struggled to find a functional solution**, and rebuilds problems that look, feel and unfold close to those — similar workspace constraints, similar behaving opponents — for spring and summer. Not replication, which is impossible; simulation.

**What each player then worked on**, versus what they had been working on:

- **Griffen** — operating closer to **movement ownership speeds**, and perceptual sensitivity to the subtle nuances of a quarterback's behaviour. Previously: his get-off from the stance and his interactions with the offensive tackle.
- **Rhodes** — **deceleration skills in context** under fuller control, face-to-face with a quarterback or back in open space, especially against feints and fakes. Previously: close 1v1 coverage nuances against receivers — line-of-scrimmage technique, speed changes, hand fighting.

**Why it works** — The insight is that a player's positional problem inventory ([[framework--position-problem-inventory]]) is necessary but not sufficient. It tells you what they face *often*. It does not tell you what beats them. Their worst plays do.

**When to apply** — Directly. At season's end, pull each athlete's three to five worst plays and build the offseason from them. For a returning athlete, the equivalent is the plays around and including the injury — with the apprehension caution from [[heuristic--right-thing-from-wrong-positions]] firmly attached.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**. Both players made the Pro Bowl again in 2017 **and** earned All-Pro honours, with the best seasons of their careers. That is an outcome, not evidence: **n = 2, no control, and elite players improve for many reasons.** The book presents it as a story about the method, not proof of it, and it should be repeated that way. Note also that three to five plays is a small, high-variance sample — a player's worst plays may reflect a scheme failure or a rare situation rather than a durable gap.

**Example** — The transferable question at a season review: **"Which three plays beat you this year?"** — then build those problems, rather than the ones the position generally presents.

When we look at isometric peak force as an output,

However, when we use the medium to long muscle lengths, we seem to have better distribution of force throughout the range of motion. So at multiple angles from short to long. Now the best gains in isometric peak force are brought about by moderate to high intensity training, which makes sense. It's a similar sort of concept with traditional training. So depending on your muscle length training, it doesn't seem to have an effect on your squat performance or your counter-moving jump performance. You can train at either short or long muscle lengths in that case. So quick summary of that evidence. There's an angle specificity. So if you train at a certain angle, that seems to be the angle that you'd adapt at the most.

87	**[29:26]** But there is definitely some cross effect, both short and long. Long muscle length has better morphological adaptation and better strength through range of motion. So multiple joints. Longer muscle length seems to be more effective at getting you stronger through your full range of motion. Now remember architectural adaptations. So things like fast going changes and panacea angle changes, they're questionable. Potentially they exist with isometric training, but they are questionable.

If you explode into the movement or should I say that the action, then you will get better from a rate of force development perspective or higher forces at shorter time periods. 93	**[31:04]** Kind of makes sense. So my journey and I guess developing or implementing run specific isometric started right back in the UK about 10 years ago. And a long story short, we're trying to convince this very successful athlete to do some neuromuscular training in the gym. And basically the only way I could do it was to use a test that we're already doing isometric mid-thigh pull and essentially putting her on one leg and asking her to pull as hard as she can over time.
94	
95	**[31:50]** Working sort of between 80 percent to 100 percent. And I just said to her, I promise you, you can be in and out of the gym in 20 minutes. Just give me that twice a week. And I reckon there's a good hunch we're going to get you better. We're going to give it better running and we're also going to make you stronger. And we're just going to use one exercise. I'll allow you to use your gloves, but we're going to strap you into the bar and you're just going to pull as hard as you possibly can. And I'm going to give you visual feedback. You're going to see your force trace. And I'm going to tell you different times as we go through a periodized plan, what level to hit on the screen. 96

So the session was she did three sets of three repetitions of four second pulls. So low duration work and relatively low volume work, to be honest. After that one athlete, I trained from an isometric standpoint, looking at performance and changes in running. I then had more exposure athletes when I returned back home to Australia and then more exposure to more running based athletes when I finally moved over to Qatar and spent four years out there in the desert, four or five years out in the desert.
98	
99	**[33:29]** Working with a host of running based athletes from team sports to athletics, middle distance runners, cross country runners to sprinters over the years. And the more I've implemented, the more I've tweaked and the more I've changed the philosophy and the more I've adapted stuff. It's been a journey. And as I said earlier on in this webinar, it's not a complete journey. It's out there for interpretation and critique. And there's a long way to go yet. But certainly at a stage now where I'm pretty happy to share run specific isometrics. It's essentially ankle, knee and hip isometrics now and also quasi isometrics. And there's a few things sort of out of the scope of this podcast, sorry, out of scope of this webinar that kind of can proceed and come after the run specific isometrics.
100	
101	**[34:19]** But nonetheless, over this journey of 10 years, I've seen significant improvements in many different physical qualities. So peak force, rate of force development or force at a certain time, leg stiffness, power output, reactive strength index. And when we're looking more specifically at the running side of things, improvements in contact time, improvements in stride length, improvements in running economy, VVO to max. Even changes in max velocity and and of course the ultimate goal where you're getting better at your performance in time trials or making personal records or better positions in race performances. There has been a number of times where I've actually come into a program, started working in the program and the only change, the only difference to the program was the implementation of the run specific isometrics. So not
102	
103	**[35:15]** exactly a controlled scientific experiment, but certainly from a coaching aspect, you know, opportunities where we've been able to look back and go, wow, that was the only thing we changed in this program and look how much better the athlete got. So I guess some good applied research as well. So probably before we get into it, it's important to kind of understand my philosophy in a real quick snapshot, a real one slider. Look, I believe that each athlete has a genetic tank and that's predetermined. Mum and dad gave you that tank and if we're doing normal training means we don't have a lot of wiggle room to change that tank very much. And what we got to do is we got to optimize what goes in that tank from a training perspective and that will give us our most optimal performance for your genetic ability.
104	
105	**[36:10]** I look at four different taps filling this tank. You know, we can at least from a strength power perspective, we can implement methods of training to improve tissue quality. That might come right down to the, you know, the morphological changes we were talking about on a tissue level, whether it's increasing fascia length or pennation angle, etc. We can turn a tap on and use an implement methods of training to increase your neuromuscular capacities, whatever that may be, maximal force output or power output, reactive strength index. So muscles, sorry, leg stiffness, if you like, we can turn a tap that succinctly works in positions and specific way a muscle might function or the way a joint angle is positioned.
106	
107	**[37:09]** So again, I guess moving over to more of a coordinate of demand and being way more specific. Or we can turn the tap on that classifier synergy. So actually doing the sporting action or very, very close to the sporting action, perhaps just applying a little bit of overload when you're doing it. And so the key to being able to implement a really good training program is understanding what taps need to be turned on. I'm not polarizing my thought. I use all four taps. In some people, all four taps are pouring at the same time. In other athletes, one taps all guns blazing while the other three are completely turned off. And I guess that's the art and partly the science, but mostly experience that sort of helps you determine and understand what taps to turn on for each athlete.
108	
109	**[38:08]** Now, when acceleration is concerned, acceleration is reasonably, dare I say, easy in terms of thinking about what taps to turn on. I mean, if you're looking at increasing tissue quality, you're probably doing some form of resistance training. I've got a squat here, but it can be anything. From a capacity standpoint, if we're looking at improving neuromuscular output in this instance, power output, we're probably going to do some explosive movement and like a squat jump here. We might work on specific positions, so knee angles or ankle angles at a set position and working a particular contraction. So in this case, just a concentric action off the box there.
110	
111	**[38:54]** And when it looks like trying to turn on more synergies, we're actually doing the event where the neuromuscular system is working co-ordinatively to execute the movement perfectly. And we can do this by adding a little bit of load, like I said, like a sled or so on. Or it might be sprinting up hills, doing hill runs, hill accelerations. Or it might actually be doing the event itself and maybe a combination of all three. But it's pretty simple to picture where each of these taps might turn on when you're looking at improving someone's acceleration ability. When it comes to max velocity running or upright running, it's very, very different.
112	
113	**[39:40]** When we're looking at general and specific options for upright running, well, there's not a lot that resembles upright running. You can essentially go and get the system strong, like I was doing with my Olympic silver medalist back in 2009, where let's just get you strong and let's hope that that increases the stiffness of your lower limbs.
114	
115	## Demands of sprint running
116	
117	**[40:06]** There's plyometric training, which is a fantastic training methodology. And it's something that I implement with my symmetrics and touch on that a little bit in a while. And ultimately, it's getting strong and doing your pliers and boom, there you go. Now go and run. So it's one side of the general spectrum, right up being quite specific with your pliers and then the actual specific events are actually running and training for your running. Some of the things we have to consider are the contact times. So when we come up with exercises, is there time to apply force and are the contact times appropriate? When we're running, there's this pretension demand when the recovery legs in the air before it comes into contact with the ground, it has to develop a level of pretension.
118	
119	**[40:57]** And a lot of the exercises we use besides pliers again, don't seem to have that demand. When you run, there's a definite contraction and then relaxation. What sort of exercises give us that ability to be able to contract hard, relatively, and then relax. Contract and relax in a rhythmical fashion. We have to consider limb velocities when you're running. The limbs are moving at a very high rate. And we don't really have anything in the gym that helps us in that context. And that's quite popular, publicized and popularized. People talk about that all the time, that nothing we can do in the gym can resemble the speeds when it comes to running.
120	
121	**[41:42]** And then of course, there's the muscle action specificity. Like, can you get that specific to what's actually happening when you're running from a muscular level? And then of course, there's very, very high unilateral forces when you run, whether you're running at 7 meters per second or 11 meters per second. The forces are actually very, very high. Can we replicate that from a general standpoint in the gym? Looking at some of Craig Purdom's work here, you can see here that almost nothing really compares to running from a force standpoint.
122	
123	**[42:28]** This is force relative to your calves, your trisobsura, your ankle muscles. When we're running at 3.5 meters per second, force is very high and it gets even higher at 5 meters per second, up to 7 meters per second. And there's nothing looking through the left hand side of the graphs. None of those bars actually come anywhere near the forces required to run, in terms of the forces that your calf is being exposed to. So we have different seated calf raises, different resistance training exercises. We even have pushing sleds like prowlers, and you even have some plyometric activities there, albeit fairly low intensity plyometric activities. They still don't seem to come up to the forces that your calf experiences when you run.
124	
125	**[43:18]** The same sort of thing, again, Craig Purdom's work here, same sort of thing with peak loading rates, that's kind of forces with a time constraint, if you like. And again, nothing compares to the running components on the right hand side of the bar graphs. So then when we look at running and a one leg isometric quarter squat, now, this certainly doesn't look specific, but at max velocity, our ground reaction forces, generally, most of the science says, they're about three times body weight. And this three times body weight forces is done in very, very short contact times. So around 90 milliseconds.
126	
127	**[44:08]** Now, if we think about an 80 kilogram male, the max force that they can put out in a one leg isometric quarter squat is around just under 4000 Newtons. That 4000 Newtons with an 80 kilogram man is about five times body weight. That's the amount of force they're able to put out five times body weight. Now, when we look at them getting to that five times body weight, and if we've instructed them to go as fast as they can to get there, then their force at 100 milliseconds is just under 3.8 times body weight, just under four times body weight.
128	
129	**[44:58]** So again, that force at 100 milliseconds is not far off. The 90 milliseconds of contact time that you have when you run and certainly the forces that they're able to exact exhibit at that time. So 100 milliseconds is well over the three times body weight that we're showing or where research is saying occurs at max velocity sprinting. So what do we have here? We basically have forces that we can train out that are applicable to max velocity running or upright running. We are essentially able to do it in the same time or near the same time. Reach those same forces. Well, for sure we can produce these in in almost identical very very similar angles and and muscle lengths.
130	
131	**[45:44]** But I guess what we don't know is what sort of muscle action is there. So we're going to do this. We're going to do this in a very similar way. We're going to do this in a very similar way. In almost identical very very similar angles and and muscle lengths. But I guess what we don't know is what sort of muscle action is there. This is an isometric muscle action. But is that the same as sprinting? Is that the same as running? When it comes to muscle function and running well. There was a belief that. Most of the muscle action that occurred here was an eccentric muscle action followed by a forceful concentric muscle action to gain flight.
132	
133	**[46:35]** But recently with some great studies particularly coming out from Adrian Lamb. I might be Adrian Lai. Might be biased because I'm Australian. But there's also some great research coming out of the states as well. Really indicating that the muscle action when we're running is isometric in nature. Or quasi isometric at worst or best depending on how you look at it. And in fact most of the most of the spring comes from tendon elongation and recoil. So essentially when we touch down on the ground we have a braking force and the muscles probably lengthen slightly I would suggest there. But then there's a strong isometric muscle action coming through to mid stance where the tendons are at their most elongated point where the center of mass drops down significantly.
134	
135	**[47:32]** And then the tendons spring us back into flight when we have our unloading phase.
136	
137	## Positions and joint-specific exercises
138	
139	**[47:43]** So when it comes to implementing the run based or run specific isometrics we have a very clear set position. And this is just look rough guides I've got from research. We're looking at five degrees of planar flexion and that's going off a zero degrees being the foot flat and standing. We're looking at 40 and 45 degree believe it or not knee extension. That's full extension being zero degrees. And we're looking at between 10 and 20 degrees of hip extension with again zero degrees being your hip fully extended in that sort of vertical standing position if you like. If we look at a sprinter and the position I'm talking about here if we see Mr. Bolt that's what I'm talking about heel kind of under hip hip under shoulder and then a middle distance athlete.
140	
141	**[48:37]** Well they're going to be pretty much the same again heel under hip hip pretty much under shoulder and again it's this mid stance position where we can see here is the highest ground reaction forces and the place where tendon is probably at its most elongated point and where you are essentially contracting your hardest in an isometric fashion. So as I started implementing my training system as you know the isometric mid thigh pull single leg was the my first go to I had reasonable success from that and then I then moved over and concentrated more on my leg.
142	
143	**[49:35]** I'm single leg isometric squat was never a big fan of testing the double leg isometric squat. I feel this forces which is too great coming through your spine for normal general sportsman but with the single leg that the forces aren't quite as high and I feel the forces are certainly higher than an isometric mid thigh pull. So I guess that gives me justification and knowing that I'm I'm for sure even in the weaker athletes still going to hit that magic three times body weight sort of threshold which is the equivalent of max velocity running ground reaction forces. So that I guess was the first development in the in the method again grit almost often see changes in max force by up to 25% of the weight.

So lower load submaximal eccentric you'd move into your super max eccentric for another couple months and then you do your holds and then your pushes and your switches and your catches as the months go on leading to the biggest competition of the year. The other way of doing it is to incorporate all of the activities submax eccentric supermaximal eccentric your holds pushes switches and catches into a four month block where you would cycle through them in a pretty quick succession and then you would repeat another block but with a different intensity and then again repeat another four month block leading into the final preparation.

**[90:50]** And that way you're not just relying on a build from one to the other that you're actually always continually hitting all of the stimulus because they've all got their unique benefits and you're hitting it regularly on four month blocks throughout a season leading up to the big one. Or another and final way of doing it is you do your four month block again exposing yourself to all of the stimuli and then you go through to a slower gradual build almost looking to peak with the ISO catch towards the end into your major competition. One way I've seen people implement this type of training to is looking at pairing it with a different running emphasis.

**[91:41]** So essentially acceleration real push concentrically dominated type activity fairly knee dominant seems to work perfectly with something like a isometric knee push amid a knee ISO push. Then we're looking at upright running max velocity full of gas running. We're looking now at an ankle ISO switch or an angle ISO catch in those sort of positions and then the gut busting speed endurance where you're just hanging on all for all dear life. Your form is getting sloppy. You're probably breaking a little bit too much now you're casting quite a lot and then it's it's all about just the hardest one which is which seems to be the hip ISO catches and the hip ISO switches and the really heavy pushes isometrically with your hips.

**[92:30]** It's one way of doing it pairing it and I probably should point out here too that isometrics for acceleration is also pretty important. Now we know there's a real concentric effort when you're accelerating and propelling yourself forward but for sure the ankle still act isolated. In fact some of the nice most locked ankles seem to be the best to be able to propel and use your hip and knee musk which are often so yes all of these isometric variance also apply to a seated calf raise position and that's depicted right here.

## Athlete case examples and conclusion

**[93:07]** So little case study even elite sprinter. So in GPP general preparation phases again no plug-in program here. How to look at what I was going to do with this particular athlete and this is essentially an example of what he was doing through GPP. We had our eccentric calf work and we had a lot of work done. In this case I exposed them to hip ISO holds and then those holds move to switches with those various loads throughout the GPP. Then moving on to SPP we moved our ankle work to ISO catches. He was prepared after really good eccentric work and he applied it to the hip.

**[94:17]** He absolutely excelled at that. That's a lot of load there leaving up to 160 kilo ankle ISO catch and his hip ISO catches too were around 35 kilos which is well over assisted weight and it became a really effective exercise for him. And also implemented something which actually comes after this isometric continuum which are literally called isometric stadium descends or ISO stadium descent. It goes like this you can apply load to this particular exercise to make it even more intense but again an isometric action with almost a cyclical component to it.

**[95:05]** So with this exercise you can apply load so you can apply this 5 kilo 10 kilo this you can use stadium steps so even larger steps. I've got a few videos of it and it's a fairly aggressive exercise again overloading running mechanics and again not something that you would just give to a developing athlete but probably more advanced than someone who's working really well through the protocol. So with this particular athlete in a case study perspective look back squat. He was a very very strong boy. He backswatted about 2.65 times body weight. See his isometric mid thigh pull in this case was very good at 5.78 so almost six times body weight that's actually really good for that position.

**[95:56]** Remember which is not as strong as the isometric squat. I hadn't quite moved on to the isometric squat at this stage. He was really good leg power is a 59, 62, 59 centimeter jumper and and over this period of time we got another 3 centimeters. So it was a meaningful change in his counter movement jump. His power output very powerful lab 6000 you know a decent change there of 200 or 2 300 watts. The speed is takeoff speed is counter movement jump and improve significantly as well. But one of the best things about the improvement of this particular athlete was his reactive strength index and now this was something that was always.

**[96:43]** Hurting the kid if you like. He wasn't very elastic. He was just a power hungry athlete. He was a big accelerator wasn't great and Max velocity wasn't very reactive and we worked very hard on not not so much as plyometrics but his isometrics which were able to be able to increase his reactive strength. And so over time we have really good changes again measured from off the jump looking at his kinematics around that 30 40 meter mark towards the end of his acceleration. So really good changes in his contact time.

**[97:35]** And when we have a look at his graph through to the 100 meters, you can see very much he was able to accelerate for longer around these patches and actually obtain a higher Max velocity. So really successful program with this guy in the implementation of isometrics to improve his reactivity is reactive strength and then also have improvements in his Max velocity running or at least supporting the track program to make the guy faster. And you can see here that his speeds are up around 11 meters per second a little bit higher than let me just per second over the last couple years. I've been collaborating with a coach over in Poland. His name is Peter Marazu ski and he's been implementing run specific isometrics very successfully with one of his elite heardlers this particular hurdler stagnate in his inner performances and I'll show you that in a second and then with the implementing implementation of run specific isometrics.

**[98:38]** We've seen a really successful gain in her performances over time. What you can see here is in brackets. My targets in this particular case for the ankle is a holds two times body weight. You can see that this particular athlete after training for a number of years now is has been able to surpass those targets. So this is another thing with the knee isa holds and me isometric pushes again implementing this training. She's been able to get stronger and stronger in those really specific isometric positions and again the same sort of thing with the hip isometrics as well. In this case remember earlier on I said you can go a long way with just using holds and pushes.

**[99:27]** Based on this athletes competencies. We will progress to the switches and catches and in fact that's coming in now as we speak. She's become very very good very strong in those specific positions holding and pushing. Remember holds and pushes having both concentric and eccentric neural pathways. We've been able to go a long way and show an example of how far we come over the last couple of years. So as I said this particular athlete would do a track training and then predominantly. Do her general strength traditional training every squatting bedlifting Olympic lifting.

**[100:13]** And the big major change to this athletes program from 2018 now moving through. Beyond halfway through 2019 has been the implementation of run-specific isometrics. What you can see is over the years as a junior elite athlete moving through the years time reducing and getting faster and faster in a hundred meter hurdles. Then you can see this stagnation around 2016 and 2017 and then we implement the run specific isometrics along with great coaching and great technical training and in the hundred meter hurdles. And we see this great reduction further to really really brought in on elite level.

**[100:58]** And from a pure speed perspective for those that are terribly interested in herdling. You can see here then over time. She had a real stagnation in her speed and she wasn't getting any faster. In fact she actually was getting slower in some some perspectives. But then you see a real change in her speed and they're getting much faster after the implementation of run specific isometrics. So again a successful use of run specific isometrics and done in the coaches own way really grasping, you know, the basis of the methodology but then applying it in his own way and collaborating collaborating with me to try and make that work really well and hats off for a really well established coach to think out of the box and try and implement that.

**[101:49]** And so far so good and successful. What I really like about this story is is the athletes by and and here's a great example of the buying. **[103:25]** It's open for critique. It's the only way we're going to get better as an industry moving forward. Yes, I've done a lot of work in it. Invite others. == latham-2026-the-effects-of-the-repetitive-use-of-a-position-specific-loading-pattern-on-lower-limb-asy.md
This was an uncontrolled short-term longitudinal study with pre-camp and late-camp testing. Athletes completed a position-specific isometric staggered-stance pull, isometric midthigh pull, ForceFrame hip abduction and adduction tests, and a countermovement jump. Limbs were classified as the offensiv
- Post-leg peak force in the isometric staggered-stance pull increased from 172.3 to 211.3 N, while the set-leg change was not statistically significant. [p. 5]
- Isometric midthigh-pull peak vertical force increased in both the post and set legs during camp, so the result was not a unilateral post-leg adaptation. [p. 5]
== bishop-2021-a-novel-approach-for-athlete-profiling-the-unilateral-dynamic-strength-index.md
tags: ["dynamic-strength-index", "unilateral-testing", "countermovement-jump", "isometric-squat", "reliability"]
The paper provides reliability and interpretation boundaries for using unilateral isometric-squat and countermovement-jump peak force to profile limb-specific strength and ballistic-force capacity.
Are unilateral isometric-squat peak force, countermovement-jump peak force, and their dynamic strength index reliable within and between sessions, and does limb definition affect the result?
== wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar.md
tags: ["hamstring", "secondary-prevention", "post-match-monitoring", "isometric-strength", "youth-football"]
Was adding regular post-match isometric hamstring-strength monitoring and individualized intervention associated with fewer and lower-burden hamstring strains in an elite youth football development program?
- Isometric hamstring peak force was tested on the first regular training day after a rest day, at least 40 hours after the match.

# Run-Specific Isometrics: Overloading What Upright Running Actually Demands

**What it is** — Natera's core argument. Upright (max-velocity) running asks for things the gym rarely supplies: brief ground contact (he cites about 90 ms), very high **unilateral** force (about 3× body weight at max velocity, "up to 5× BW" registered), pre-tension before touchdown, rhythmic contract–relax, and a stiff ankle. Bilateral lifts, seated calf raises, sleds and low-level plyos all fall short of running's calf forces (he shows Craig Purdam's data, ~42:28). A **single-leg isometric quarter squat** closes that gap. His worked example is an 80 kg male: peak force just under 4000 N (about 5× BW), and when he is told to explode, about 3.8× BW at 100 ms. So in roughly the time of a sprint contact, the athlete exceeds sprint GRF, at a sprint-like joint angle, on one leg. *(Numbers come from a single-source ASR transcript and are unconfirmed. Verify at ~43:18–45:44.)*

**Why it works** — The mechanism is **asserted, not shown**. Natera cites newer work (probably Adrian Lai et al.; the ASR hears "Adrian Lamb/Lai") suggesting the stance muscle action in running is isometric or quasi-isometric: the muscle holds length through mid-stance while the tendon stretches and recoils to supply most of the "spring." If that is true, training high-force isometrics at mid-stance angles matches both the muscle action and the force level. He concedes the open question himself (~45:44): equal force and equal angle do not prove the same muscle function, so they do not prove transfer. He adds a cost case against traditional lifting (~13:33–18:28), all stated as coaching experience:
- low energy cost and little mechanical damage, so athletes recover same-day or next-day;
- sessions rarely run past 10–15 min, so they can be trained often, even week to week in season;
- low technical demand and an analgesic effect;
- little hypertrophy with his parameters;
- strength carries about ±15° beyond the trained angle (his figure is from "coaching manuals").

**When to apply** — The athlete is already strong and sprints well, but max velocity or reactivity has stalled; Natera calls this an "outside the box" option, not a first step. It also fits in-season college football skill players who need a high-force stimulus but cannot absorb heavy bilateral loading between games. It suits calf/Achilles-conscious athletes because it loads high force with little movement. **Force-plate hook:** a single-leg isometric squat on ForceDecks gives peak force (as ×BW) and force at 100 ms. Compare them with the ~3× BW sprint-GRF threshold. An athlete who cannot reach ~3× BW by 100 ms has a measurable gap.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use it in place of sprinting, conventional strength work or plyometrics; Natera says "the bread and butter of traditional training methods certainly come first." Do not use it with novices, who have not exhausted cheaper general methods. It is not a hypertrophy tool. Its transfer to sprint speed is **untested**: every performance change he reports is a coaching observation made during concurrent training (see [[case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler]]). He also says the "3–5× BW" running-GRF figures come from the literature, but on these slides they are paraphrased by ASR. Do not quote them as measured values.

**Example** — An 80 kg receiver produces 3,700 N (4.7× BW) peak on a single-leg iso squat, but only 2,100 N (2.7× BW) at 100 ms. His max force is fine and his early force is the gap. That points to explosive-intent pushes, not heavier grinding.

Provenance: the lesson is a ~2019 rugbystrengthcoach.com webinar (host Keir) repackaged in Moyer's course (Vimeo 352094174).

**Related** — [[claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]] — the ankle-force premise behind the ankle variants.

# Isometric Training Variables and the Adaptations They Bias

**What it is** — Five dials set an isometric stimulus. Natera maps each one to adaptations using a review that the ASR renders as "Orren Schuch." It is almost certainly **Oranchuk, Storey, Nelson & Cronin (2019), *Isometric training and long-term adaptations: effects of muscle length, intensity and intent*** (Scand J Med Sci Sports); two papers in Zotero cite it under that title.
- **Duration.** Short is 2–6 s, moderate about 10 s, long 20–30 s.
- **Muscle length.** Short, moderate or long.
- **Intent.** "Grind" means ramping to maximal force; "explode" means ballistic, reaching force as fast as possible.
- **Intensity.** Low is 30–50% of max; high is 70–100%.
- **Volume.** Reps × sets × duration.

His summary of the review (~22:15–30:14):
- **Muscle mass** is favored by long lengths, higher volume, grind intent and long holds.
- **Fascicle length** changes are equivocal, and length does not change the result. Long lengths favor a **pennation angle** increase.
- **Tendon cross-sectional area and stiffness** respond to high intensity (≥70%), long lengths and **ballistic intent**. Duration matters little, with long "slightly better" for stiffness.
- **Neural adaptation follows intent.** Grind raises EMG at maximal voluntary contraction; explode raises EMG at 0–100 and 100–150 ms.
- **Peak force** does not differ by length. Moderate-to-long lengths spread gains across more of the range, and moderate-to-high intensity gives the best gains.
- **Rate of force development** improves with ballistic intent.
- **Dynamic performance** (squat, CMJ) shows little difference by length or intent.
- **Angle specificity** holds, with some carryover to both shorter and longer lengths.

*(Single-source ASR; verify the slide wording at ~22:15–30:14 and against the paper itself.)*

**Why it works** — Specificity: the tissue and the nervous system adapt to the stimulus they are given. Natera then **selects** from this map for running (~56:03–59:16):
- explode-to-max intent, for tendon and RFD, which also limits hypertrophy;
- **moderate** muscle lengths, avoiding both short lengths and the hypertrophic long end;
- near-max to max intensities (70–100%);
- short holds and low volume, to avoid hypertrophy and fatigue.

He says the method came first and he found the evidence afterward. The link between "moderate length + ballistic" and "better sprint tissue" is his inference, not a tested outcome.

**When to apply** — Use it to reason about *which* dial to turn for a stated goal. Examples: the tendon stiffness bias for an Achilles or patellar tendon RTP late in rehab; RFD for a skill player whose force at 100 ms lags his peak; long, heavier holds in early offseason GPP, when some muscle mass is welcome. **Force-plate hook:** ForceDecks isometric tests separate peak force from force at 50/100/200 ms, so you can check whether an explode block actually moved early force rather than peak force.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one coach's paraphrase of one review, heard through ASR. Read Oranchuk 2019 before citing any single cell of the map. Much of the review's evidence comes from single-joint lab studies in untrained or recreationally trained subjects, so how it generalizes to trained sprinters is unknown. Architecture changes are "questionable," as Natera says himself. Tendon claims (intensity ≥70%, ballistic intent) are **tissue-adaptation claims, untested in this context**. Do not apply the early-rehab analgesic-isometric literature (Rio/Cook) here; that is a different goal with different dosing.

**Example** — For a DB coming off a patellar tendinopathy flare, pick high intensity (≥70%), ballistic intent, moderate knee angle and short 3 s efforts at low volume. That prescription follows from this map; it is not a validated protocol.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-push-hold-switch-catch-continuum]] — how the dials are applied in practice.

# Run-Specific Isometric Set Positions: Ankle, Knee, Hip

**What it is** — Every run-specific isometric (RSI) is **unilateral**, performed at the **mid-stance** position of upright running: heel under hip, hip under shoulder. That is where GRF peaks and the tendon is presumably most stretched. Natera's "rough guides from research" (~47:43):
- **Ankle:** about 5° plantar flexion (0° = foot flat), so the heel sits just off the floor.
- **Knee:** 40–45° flexion (0° = full extension). In practice he sets 35–40°, "a little shallow."
- **Hip:** 10–20° extension (0° = standing vertical).

The equipment is a **Smith machine** (the first thing he asks for at a new job), or an overloaded barbell in a solid rack, with a **force plate** underneath for feedback and load setting. *(Angles from single-source ASR; verify at ~47:43 and on the setup demos at ~60:56–65:42.)*

**Why it works** — Angle specificity: strength gains concentrate near the trained angle. Training at the mid-stance angle puts the strength where sprint GRF peaks. The setup cues all exist to **isolate the target joint** so that the measured force belongs to it:
- **Ankle push:** lock the knee completely. With any bend, the quads take over, scores come out artificially high, and every later load calculated from them overshoots "by a long way." Cue "calf raise as hard and aggressively as you can."
- **Knee push:** bar in a high back-squat position; feet hip-width apart.
- **Hip push:** a bridge with the bar across the hip crease, and three contact points: the lower shoulder blade on a softer box, the heel on a hard box or force plate, and the knee slightly flexed (about 40° or straighter). Keep the heel dorsiflexed and the body horizontally "stacked."
- **All three:** keep the swing leg in front of the stance leg for specificity, although he is "not too anal" about knee height.

**When to apply** — Use this when building any unilateral isometric test or training station. In football the knee and ankle stations are easy to add to a ForceDecks testing day. A single-leg iso squat at 35–40° knee flexion is a reasonable, repeatable position to track across a calf or quad RTP and back to baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — The angles describe **upright** sprint mid-stance. Acceleration stance is more flexed, so these angles are not specific to the first steps. None of the three positions targets the **hamstrings as knee flexors** or at long length; the hip bridge is the nearest, and it is still a hip-extension task. Do not treat these positions as hamstring RTP tests. Natera accepts about ±5° error, so the angles are not precise targets. The single-leg bilateral-free setup and the **hip "system weight" (~33% BW)** convention need careful calculation, or ratios will not be comparable across athletes.

**Example** — Ankle station: Smith bar on the shoulders, the athlete stands tall on one leg on a ForceDecks plate with the knee locked, rises to about 5° plantar flexion, and **pushes to max while the coach sets the bar stops**. That removes soft-tissue slack, so the position is set under load and not at rest.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-push-hold-switch-catch-continuum]] — the four exercise types run in these positions.

# Isometric Training Variables and the Adaptations They Bias

**What it is** — Five dials set an isometric stimulus. Natera maps each one to adaptations using a review that the ASR renders as "Orren Schuch." It is almost certainly **Oranchuk, Storey, Nelson & Cronin (2019), *Isometric training and long-term adaptations: effects of muscle length, intensity and intent*** (Scand J Med Sci Sports); two papers in Zotero cite it under that title.
- **Duration.** Short is 2–6 s, moderate about 10 s, long 20–30 s.
- **Muscle length.** Short, moderate or long.
- **Intent.** "Grind" means ramping to maximal force; "explode" means ballistic, reaching force as fast as possible.
- **Intensity.** Low is 30–50% of max; high is 70–100%.
- **Volume.** Reps × sets × duration.

His summary of the review (~22:15–30:14):
- **Muscle mass** is favored by long lengths, higher volume, grind intent and long holds.
- **Fascicle length** changes are equivocal, and length does not change the result. Long lengths favor a **pennation angle** increase.
- **Tendon cross-sectional area and stiffness** respond to high intensity (≥70%), long lengths and **ballistic intent**. Duration matters little, with long "slightly better" for stiffness.
- **Neural adaptation follows intent.** Grind raises EMG at maximal voluntary contraction; explode raises EMG at 0–100 and 100–150 ms.
- **Peak force** does not differ by length. Moderate-to-long lengths spread gains across more of the range, and moderate-to-high intensity gives the best gains.
- **Rate of force development** improves with ballistic intent.
- **Dynamic performance** (squat, CMJ) shows little difference by length or intent.
- **Angle specificity** holds, with some carryover to both shorter and longer lengths.

*(Single-source ASR; verify the slide wording at ~22:15–30:14 and against the paper itself.)*

**Why it works** — Specificity: the tissue and the nervous system adapt to the stimulus they are given. Natera then **selects** from this map for running (~56:03–59:16):
- explode-to-max intent, for tendon and RFD, which also limits hypertrophy;
- **moderate** muscle lengths, avoiding both short lengths and the hypertrophic long end;
- near-max to max intensities (70–100%);
- short holds and low volume, to avoid hypertrophy and fatigue.

He says the method came first and he found the evidence afterward. The link between "moderate length + ballistic" and "better sprint tissue" is his inference, not a tested outcome.

**When to apply** — Use it to reason about *which* dial to turn for a stated goal. Examples: the tendon stiffness bias for an Achilles or patellar tendon RTP late in rehab; RFD for a skill player whose force at 100 ms lags his peak; long, heavier holds in early offseason GPP, when some muscle mass is welcome. **Force-plate hook:** ForceDecks isometric tests separate peak force from force at 50/100/200 ms, so you can check whether an explode block actually moved early force rather than peak force.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one coach's paraphrase of one review, heard through ASR. Read Oranchuk 2019 before citing any single cell of the map. Much of the review's evidence comes from single-joint lab studies in untrained or recreationally trained subjects, so how it generalizes to trained sprinters is unknown. Architecture changes are "questionable," as Natera says himself. Tendon claims (intensity ≥70%, ballistic intent) are **tissue-adaptation claims, untested in this context**. Do not apply the early-rehab analgesic-isometric literature (Rio/Cook) here; that is a different goal with different dosing.

**Example** — For a DB coming off a patellar tendinopathy flare, pick high intensity (≥70%), ballistic intent, moderate knee angle and short 3 s efforts at low volume. That prescription follows from this map; it is not a validated protocol.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-push-hold-switch-catch-continuum]] — how the dials are applied in practice.

# Run-Specific Isometric Set Positions: Ankle, Knee, Hip

**What it is** — Every run-specific isometric (RSI) is **unilateral**, performed at the **mid-stance** position of upright running: heel under hip, hip under shoulder. That is where GRF peaks and the tendon is presumably most stretched. Natera's "rough guides from research" (~47:43):
- **Ankle:** about 5° plantar flexion (0° = foot flat), so the heel sits just off the floor.
- **Knee:** 40–45° flexion (0° = full extension). In practice he sets 35–40°, "a little shallow."
- **Hip:** 10–20° extension (0° = standing vertical).

The equipment is a **Smith machine** (the first thing he asks for at a new job), or an overloaded barbell in a solid rack, with a **force plate** underneath for feedback and load setting. *(Angles from single-source ASR; verify at ~47:43 and on the setup demos at ~60:56–65:42.)*

**Why it works** — Angle specificity: strength gains concentrate near the trained angle. Training at the mid-stance angle puts the strength where sprint GRF peaks. The setup cues all exist to **isolate the target joint** so that the measured force belongs to it:
- **Ankle push:** lock the knee completely. With any bend, the quads take over, scores come out artificially high, and every later load calculated from them overshoots "by a long way." Cue "calf raise as hard and aggressively as you can."
- **Knee push:** bar in a high back-squat position; feet hip-width apart.
- **Hip push:** a bridge with the bar across the hip crease, and three contact points: the lower shoulder blade on a softer box, the heel on a hard box or force plate, and the knee slightly flexed (about 40° or straighter). Keep the heel dorsiflexed and the body horizontally "stacked."
- **All three:** keep the swing leg in front of the stance leg for specificity, although he is "not too anal" about knee height.

**When to apply** — Use this when building any unilateral isometric test or training station. In football the knee and ankle stations are easy to add to a ForceDecks testing day. A single-leg iso squat at 35–40° knee flexion is a reasonable, repeatable position to track across a calf or quad RTP and back to baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — The angles describe **upright** sprint mid-stance. Acceleration stance is more flexed, so these angles are not specific to the first steps. None of the three positions targets the **hamstrings as knee flexors** or at long length; the hip bridge is the nearest, and it is still a hip-extension task. Do not treat these positions as hamstring RTP tests. Natera accepts about ±5° error, so the angles are not precise targets. The single-leg bilateral-free setup and the **hip "system weight" (~33% BW)** convention need careful calculation, or ratios will not be comparable across athletes.

**Example** — Ankle station: Smith bar on the shoulders, the athlete stands tall on one leg on a ForceDecks plate with the knee locked, rises to about 5° plantar flexion, and **pushes to max while the coach sets the bar stops**. That removes soft-tissue slack, so the position is set under load and not at rest.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-push-hold-switch-catch-continuum]] — the four exercise types run in these positions.

# The Isometric Continuum: Push → Hold → Switch → Catch

**What it is** — Natera uses four exercise types, all in the same set positions, arranged by rising task intensity (~59:20–80:17):
1. **ISO push.** A near-max to max push into an immovable bar, with either explode intent (rapid, momentary) or grind intent (built in about three steps to max). This is also the **test**: every other load is derived from it. Training dose is 0.5–3 s efforts. At 80–90% he does 3 s efforts with more reps; at true max, few reps and few sets.
2. **ISO hold.** The athlete supports body mass plus an external load in the set position. It is **necessarily submaximal**, because free weight is less stable than a fixed bar and gives no time to ramp up. Handed 100% of push capacity, the athlete buckles. Heavy holds last about 3 s (3–5 s); lighter, longer holds sit in early GPP.
3. **ISO switch** (quasi-isometric). The limbs switch, the athlete lands in the set position and briefly holds. External load drops sharply because "the demands of the free limb" raise the intensity. He uses 3 reps at heavier loads and 5 at lighter, for 2–3 sets.
4. **ISO catch** (quasi-isometric). A small drop or hop into the position, caught and held. This carries the lowest external load and the highest GRF. At high loads it is catch-and-go; at lighter loads a brief hold follows.

The central point: **as the task gets more dynamic, the external weight falls but GRF rises.** Natera's knee-catch figures for an 80 kg athlete with about 5 cm of displacement: ~6× BW landing force with a 40 kg load and ~8× BW with 80 kg. At ~10 cm with 80 kg: just over 11× BW. At ~15 cm: ~14× BW. Running GRF, by contrast, is "registered up to 5× BW." *(Single-source ASR; the tables are on slides. Verify at ~74:15–76:50.)*

**Why it works** — The GRF rise is plain impulse–momentum physics: landing from a height forces the body to stop in a very short time. Natera's **neural claim** is different and **only asserted**: pushes share neural pathways with *concentric* actions and holds share them with *eccentric* actions, so the two drive different adaptations. He says so himself: "there's a lot more science hopefully to come… you might just have to rely on my spiel for now" (~68:13). Switches and catches are only quasi-isometric; some lengthening occurs, and it becomes **visible when the load is too high or the athlete lacks competence**. That visible yielding is his practical failure signal.

**When to apply** — Use the order as a progression gate for any athlete returning to high-speed running. Pushes and holds come first because they are controlled, testable and high force. Switches and catches are the bridge toward reactive, running-like loading. **Force-plate hook:**
- **Pushes:** peak force and force at 100 ms.
- **Catches:** landing peak force and time to stabilization. This shows whether a catch at a given load is actually producing the intended ×BW, rather than relying on Natera's displacement table.

**When NOT to apply** — Catches are **advanced**. Natera has taken only about 7–8 athletes that far (see [[heuristic--isometric-pushes-and-holds-are-destinations]]). The 6–14× BW landing forces exceed running GRF by design; they are inappropriate for a healing tendon or muscle, an athlete who is short on eccentric preparation, or anyone showing yield on landing. The push/hold "neural pathway" distinction is a hypothesis. Do not justify the programming choice from it alone.

**Example** — An 80 kg athlete, knee position ([[heuristic--derive-isometric-loads-from-the-push-test]]): the push registers 2,943 N total (about 3.75× BW). The knee **catch** with only ~60 kg external load registers about 5,547 N (about 7× BW). Much less on the bar, nearly double the force.

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-set-positions-ankle-knee-hip]] — the positions every type uses.

# Derive Every Isometric Load from the Push Test

**What it is** — Test first. The maximal isometric **push** at each joint sets capacity, and hold, switch and catch loads step down from it (~54:33–80:17). **Read the units carefully.** The push benchmarks are **total force, including body weight**. The hold, switch and catch figures are **external load on the bar**.

**Capacity benchmarks for "well to very well trained, not elite" athletes** (push, total force):
- **Ankle** (knee locked): 2.75–3× BW at ~54:33, but **2.75–3.5× BW** at ~71:32. The two statements disagree, so both are recorded here.
- **Knee:** 3.75–5× BW.
- **Hip:** 2.5–3.5× **system weight**, where system weight is the ~33% of body mass supported in the bridge. That comes to about 1× BW.

**Step-down ratios he states** (external load):
- Ankle hold: 1.5–2× BW.
- Knee hold: +2 to +3× BW.
- Knee switch: +1 to +2× BW.
- Catches: about +0.5 to +1× BW, less when more airborne.

**His worked table for an 80 kg "average, trained" athlete** (external kg; push shown as force registered minus body weight):

| Joint | Push | Hold | Switch | Catch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ankle | 140 | 120 | 80 | 60 |
| Knee | 220 | 160 | 80 | 60 |
| Hip | 40 | 33 | 26 | 13 |

**Arithmetic check** — The table is internally consistent, which raises confidence in the ASR here.
- Ankle: 140 + 80 = 220 kg = 2.75× BW.
- Knee: 220 + 80 = 300 kg = 3.75× BW, and 300 × 9.81 = 2,943 N, the exact figure he quotes.
- Hip: 40 + ~26 kg system weight ≈ 66 kg ≈ 2.5× system.
- Holds: 120 kg = 1.5× BW (ankle) and 160 kg = 2× BW (knee), both inside his stated ranges.

# Isometric Pushes and Holds Are Destinations, Not Waypoints

**What it is** — "The risk of putting out a continuum there is people think **completing versus competence**, and it's always about competence" (~89:39). Most athletes keep improving on pushes and holds alone. Natera has taken only "maybe seven or eight" athletes all the way to catches (~76:50). A less developed athlete might stay at holds, with some pushes, "for the first two years." He moves an athlete on **only when adaptation stalls and competence is shown**. "There's no rush."

**Why it works** — The next stage adds landing forces far above running GRF (catches reach 6–14× BW) and eccentric yielding. If the current stage still produces gains, advancing adds risk without adding stimulus. The gate he uses is observable: can the athlete **hold the position under the load**? Visible lengthening or buckling in a switch or catch means the load is too high or the athlete lacks competence. This is coaching logic, and it is consistent with ordinary progressive-overload practice. The specific stage-duration claims are his experience.

**When to apply** — Use it as the default stance for football. Most rosters, and nearly all true freshmen, live at pushes and holds. Advance to switches only when both of these hold:
1. push-derived capacity has plateaued across two test points on ForceDecks;
2. holds show no position loss at the target load.

In RTP, keep the athlete at pushes and holds through the late-rehab strength phase, and treat switches and catches as a separate, later decision made alongside the high-speed running progression.

**When NOT to apply** — "Destination" does not mean *never* progress. An advanced sprinter who has stalled on holds may need the reactive stimulus, as Natera's elite sprinter did (see [[case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler]]). The "two years at holds" figure and the "7–8 athletes" count are anecdotal, ASR-transcribed and **unverified** (~76:50, ~88:49). They are not development norms.

**Example** — The hurdler case: after roughly 18 months of holds and pushes only, she had exceeded her ankle-hold target of 2× BW, and switches and catches were "coming in now as we speak."

**Related** — [[framework--isometric-push-hold-switch-catch-continuum]] — the stages this gates.

# Eccentric-to-Isometric Periodization for Team Sport

**What it is** — Natera sketches two team-sport annual plans (~80:44–88:49) and stresses that they are **not plug-in programs**.

**Plan A: eccentric-led.**
- **Offseason:** about 80% of the strength stimulus is eccentric and 10–20% isometric. It opens with long time-under-tension eccentrics at 80–100% RM and longer-duration holds that build toward their load.
- **Then:** ISO pushes enter as grind training at 3–5 s, and the eccentrics move to 4–6 s above 1RM.
- **Around December–January:** supramaximal eccentrics at **110–140%**, 2–4 s. Pushes shift from grind toward explode, and switches and then catches come in.
- **In season:** mostly isometric, with minimal eccentric exposure.

**Plan B: "passive" eccentric emphasis,** for high-volume team sport. It runs low-level isotonic work, then eccentrics from high-volume/light to lower-volume/heavier. Holds follow from about Oct/Nov for roughly two months, switches from mid-January, and catches from mid-March to April. **Volume stays flat and load and exercise intensity carry the progression.**

In both plans, **plyometrics continue throughout**. They are graded on a five-level arbitrary intensity scale, with emphasis splits such as 70/30 and 60/40 between high and low levels. *(Month names reflect his calendar, likely a Southern-hemisphere or Qatar season; all numbers are single-source ASR from slides. Verify at ~81:35–88:02.)*

**Why it works** — The mechanism is **asserted**. "A failed isometric muscle action is essentially an eccentric action," so heavy eccentric work prepares the athlete for high-force isometrics. Late in the year, **holds and quasi-isometrics can stand in for eccentric work**: switches and catches involve some lengthening, and holds (in his claim) share eccentric neural pathways. He reports that eccentric adaptations "stay around" when switches and catches are kept in. That is an observation, not a measured result.

**When to apply** — Fit the structure to the college football year:
- **Winter and early spring:** eccentric-heavy, holds introduced.
- **Summer:** pushes and switches.
- **Fall camp and season:** mostly isometric (pushes, holds, some switches), with short, low-soreness sessions that coexist with game-week running loads.

For staff who are uneasy about heavy eccentrics in season, this gives a rationale for replacing them with holds. **Force-plate hook:** track single-leg iso push peak force and a drop-jump RSI across the season to see whether in-season isometrics actually preserve offseason gains.

**When NOT to apply** — The whole structure is **untested**. It is one coach's template with no comparison group, and the "holds replace eccentrics" and "adaptations stay around" claims are the least supported parts. Supramaximal eccentrics at 110–140% are a real soreness and strain risk in contact-sport camps, so they need a staff with the equipment and experience. The month-by-month placement belongs to his season and needs remapping. It does **not** cover hamstring-specific eccentric work (Nordics); do not read "in season mostly isometric" as permission to drop hamstring eccentrics. For that, see the hamstring-monitoring evidence in [[wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]].

**Example** — For a Power-4 skill group: January–March, eccentric squats and RDLs with ISO holds added in March. Summer, knee and ankle ISO pushes twice weekly, switches for veterans only. From August, one or two 10–15 min isometric sessions per week plus graded plyos, with Nordics kept.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-pushes-and-holds-are-destinations]] — the development-stage version of the same plan.

# Eccentric-to-Isometric Periodization for Team Sport

**What it is** — Natera sketches two team-sport annual plans (~80:44–88:49) and stresses that they are **not plug-in programs**.

**Plan A: eccentric-led.**
- **Offseason:** about 80% of the strength stimulus is eccentric and 10–20% isometric. It opens with long time-under-tension eccentrics at 80–100% RM and longer-duration holds that build toward their load.
- **Then:** ISO pushes enter as grind training at 3–5 s, and the eccentrics move to 4–6 s above 1RM.
- **Around December–January:** supramaximal eccentrics at **110–140%**, 2–4 s. Pushes shift from grind toward explode, and switches and then catches come in.
- **In season:** mostly isometric, with minimal eccentric exposure.

**Plan B: "passive" eccentric emphasis,** for high-volume team sport. It runs low-level isotonic work, then eccentrics from high-volume/light to lower-volume/heavier. Holds follow from about Oct/Nov for roughly two months, switches from mid-January, and catches from mid-March to April. **Volume stays flat and load and exercise intensity carry the progression.**

In both plans, **plyometrics continue throughout**. They are graded on a five-level arbitrary intensity scale, with emphasis splits such as 70/30 and 60/40 between high and low levels. *(Month names reflect his calendar, likely a Southern-hemisphere or Qatar season; all numbers are single-source ASR from slides. Verify at ~81:35–88:02.)*

**Why it works** — The mechanism is **asserted**. "A failed isometric muscle action is essentially an eccentric action," so heavy eccentric work prepares the athlete for high-force isometrics. Late in the year, **holds and quasi-isometrics can stand in for eccentric work**: switches and catches involve some lengthening, and holds (in his claim) share eccentric neural pathways. He reports that eccentric adaptations "stay around" when switches and catches are kept in. That is an observation, not a measured result.

**When to apply** — Fit the structure to the college football year:
- **Winter and early spring:** eccentric-heavy, holds introduced.
- **Summer:** pushes and switches.
- **Fall camp and season:** mostly isometric (pushes, holds, some switches), with short, low-soreness sessions that coexist with game-week running loads.

For staff who are uneasy about heavy eccentrics in season, this gives a rationale for replacing them with holds. **Force-plate hook:** track single-leg iso push peak force and a drop-jump RSI across the season to see whether in-season isometrics actually preserve offseason gains.

**When NOT to apply** — The whole structure is **untested**. It is one coach's template with no comparison group, and the "holds replace eccentrics" and "adaptations stay around" claims are the least supported parts. Supramaximal eccentrics at 110–140% are a real soreness and strain risk in contact-sport camps, so they need a staff with the equipment and experience. The month-by-month placement belongs to his season and needs remapping. It does **not** cover hamstring-specific eccentric work (Nordics); do not read "in season mostly isometric" as permission to drop hamstring eccentrics. For that, see the hamstring-monitoring evidence in [[wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]].

**Example** — For a Power-4 skill group: January–March, eccentric squats and RDLs with ISO holds added in March. Summer, knee and ankle ISO pushes twice weekly, switches for veterans only. From August, one or two 10–15 min isometric sessions per week plus graded plyos, with Nordics kept.

**Related** — [[heuristic--isometric-pushes-and-holds-are-destinations]] — the development-stage version of the same plan.

# Pair the Isometric Variant with the Day's Running Emphasis

**What it is** — Natera describes, as something he has "seen people implement" (~91:41), matching the isometric variant to the running quality being trained:
- **Acceleration**, which is push-dominant, concentric and knee-dominant, pairs with the **knee ISO push**.
- **Upright or max-velocity running** pairs with the **ankle ISO switch or ankle ISO catch**.
- **Speed endurance**, where form degrades with more braking and casting, pairs with the hardest variants: **hip ISO switches and catches** and heavy hip pushes.

He adds that the ankle also acts isometrically during acceleration ("the most locked ankles seem to be the best"), so ankle work serves acceleration too, including in a **seated calf-raise** position (~92:30).

For **track athletes' annual plans** (~89:39–90:50) he gives three structures:
1. **Long sequential blocks:** submax eccentric → supramax eccentric → holds → pushes → switches → catches, building to the major championship.
2. **Repeated ~4-month blocks** that cycle through every stimulus quickly, then repeat at a different intensity, "so you're always continually hitting all of the stimulus."
3. **Hybrid:** one full cycling block, then a slow build peaking with ISO catches into the major competition.

*(Single-source ASR; verify at ~89:39–92:30.)*

**Why it works** — Specificity by phase of stance: knee extensors dominate the propulsive, flexed acceleration stance, ankle stiffness dominates the short upright contact, and hip extensors fight the breakdown seen when fatigued. This is **coaching logic, not tested pairing**. There is no evidence here that pairing beats random assignment.

**When to apply** — Use it for session design when isometrics sit on the same day as speed work. For football: knee pushes on acceleration or short-sprint days early in the week, ankle switches on max-velocity (flying 10–20 yd) days for skill players, and hip variants for positions that repeat long efforts on special teams. Order and fatigue are not addressed in the talk. A reasonable default is to run first and do isometrics afterward, keeping sprint quality high.

**When NOT to apply** — It is **untested** and secondhand ("one way I've seen people implement this"). Speed-endurance work is a small part of football conditioning. Hip catches are the most demanding variant, so do not add them to fatigued athletes just to "match" a speed-endurance day. The track block structures assume a single championship peak and a long annual cycle, which does not fit a 12–15 game season.

**Example** — Max-velocity Thursday for WRs: three flying 20s, then 2 × 3 ankle ISO switches per leg at ~1× BW external (for an 80 kg athlete, per Natera's table), with the landing checked on a force plate.

**Related** — [[framework--eccentric-to-isometric-periodization-team-sport]] — the team-sport annual version.

# Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics

**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).

**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).

**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."

*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*

**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.

**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.

**Example** — Screening question for a strong-but-stiff-less athlete: "Is this athlete's RSI low relative to his iso push ×BW?" If yes, he fits the sprinter case, and Natera would add ankle switches and catches after an eccentric calf base.

**Related** — [[principle--isometric-overload-for-upright-running]] — the rationale these cases are offered to illustrate.

# Unilateral Isometrics Expose Asymmetries That Bilateral Tests Hide

**What it is** — Natera shows one athlete tested on dual force plates (~18:28–19:18). Bilateral countermovement-jump and squat asymmetries looked unremarkable, "that you wouldn't particularly be too worried about." When the athlete was tested **one leg at a time isometrically**, the asymmetries "appear pretty significantly." He calls these "hidden" asymmetries: bilateral lifts let the stronger limb compensate. *(The magnitudes are on the slide and not in the audio; verify at ~18:28.)*

**Why it works** — In a bilateral task the total output can be preserved by redistributing force to the stronger side, so the between-limb split understates the true deficit. A unilateral maximal isometric test removes that option and isolates each limb's capacity. The idea is well established in RTP testing (post-ACL work shows it in explosive strength). Natera offers a single illustration, not data.

**When to apply** — Use it in the return-to-play and preseason screening of football players. A clean bilateral CMJ asymmetry on ForceDecks should not end the screen after a lower-limb injury: add a **single-leg isometric squat** or an ankle push in the run-specific positions, on each leg. It also fits the unilateral dynamic strength index approach ([[bishop-2021-a-novel-approach-for-athlete-profiling-the-unilateral-dynamic-strength-index]]), which pairs single-leg iso squat and CMJ peak force. That paper also sets the reliability limits to respect before calling a small difference real.

**When NOT to apply** — One slide, one athlete, no magnitudes given, so it is **supported** only because it agrees with the wider literature. Not every unilateral asymmetry matters. Position-specific asymmetries can be sport-driven and may not be deficits: [[latham-2026-the-effects-of-the-repetitive-use-of-a-position-specific-loading-pattern-on-lower-limb-asy]] reports limb-specific changes from football stance loading. # Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics

**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).

**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).

**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."

*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*

**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.

**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.

**Example** — Screening question for a strong-but-stiff-less athlete: "Is this athlete's RSI low relative to his iso push ×BW?" If yes, he fits the sprinter case, and Natera would add ankle switches and catches after an eccentric calf base.

**Related** — [[principle--isometric-overload-for-upright-running]] — the rationale these cases are offered to illustrate.

# Hamstrings Are Not Purely Isometric in Late Swing (Contested)

**What it is** — Moyer's position in a live debate. One camp (he names Frans Bosch and "research out of Holland," using animal and computer-modelling work) holds that the hamstrings act **quasi-isometrically** through swing, with the tendon doing the lengthening and shortening. Moyer says there is "enough evidence" that they are **not fully isometric**: he accepts a quasi-isometric component but argues for real **eccentric and concentric** phases — eccentric to stop the thigh in mid-to-late swing, then pulling the leg down and back (pawback). He cites a 2020 review, **unnamed in the transc

**Why it works** — If the muscle fascicles do change length meaningfully, isometric-only training would miss the eccentric braking and the fast switch to shortening in the injury-prone window. **His main argument does not settle this.** "Two joints are moving, so the muscle can't be isometric" is about the **muscle-tendon unit**, whose lengthening nobody disputes; the Bosch camp's position is about the **fascicles**, with the tendon absorbing the length change. So he argues past the other camp. The question turns on fascicle-level data during high-speed sprinting, which are scarce.
